overview: dbt tests are automated assertions about your data: statements like 'this column is never null', 'these values are unique', or 'every order points at a real customer'. dbt turns each assertion into a SQL query that selects the rows that violate the rule. If that query returns zero rows, the test passes; if it returns any rows, the test fails and dbt reports how many bad rows it found. This 'find the failing rows' model is the single most important idea in dbt testing - a test is just a query for bad data.

There are two flavors. Generic tests are parameterized, reusable tests attached to a column or model in YAML - the four built-in ones are not_null, unique, accepted_values, and relationships - and you can write your own generic tests as macros. Singular tests are one-off SQL files in the tests/ directory: you write a bespoke SELECT that returns the rows you consider wrong, and dbt runs it as-is. Generic tests cover the common, repeatable rules; singular tests handle the specific, complex logic that does not generalize.

You run tests with dbt test (or as part of dbt build, which interleaves models and their tests). Each test has a severity - error (fail the build) or warn (report but keep going) - and you can set thresholds with error_if and warn_if to only fail when the number of failing rows crosses a limit. In CI, tests run automatically on every pull request so bad data or broken logic is caught before it reaches production dashboards. Packages like dbt_utils and dbt_expectations add dozens more ready-made generic tests.
learningObjectives: Explain the core dbt testing model - a test is a query that returns failing rows, passing when zero rows come back - and configure the four built-in generic tests (not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships) in YAML.
Write custom generic tests as macros and singular tests as SQL files in tests/, and control severity and thresholds with error/warn, error_if, and warn_if, plus store_failures for debugging.
Run tests with dbt test and dbt build, wire tests into CI so they gate pull requests, and extend coverage with the dbt_utils and dbt_expectations test packages.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A dbt test is a data-quality assertion that dbt compiles into a SQL query returning the rows that violate the assertion; a test passes when the query returns zero rows and fails otherwise (the failing row count is reported). Generic tests are parameterized tests defined as macros (built-in: not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships) and applied declaratively in YAML under a model's or column's tests: key; dbt renders the macro with the supplied arguments to produce the failing-rows query. Singular tests are standalone .sql files in the tests/ directory containing a SELECT statement whose result set is the set of failing rows. Tests are executed by dbt test (standalone) or dbt build (interleaved with model runs), each carrying a config with severity ('error' or 'warn'), optional error_if/warn_if thresholds (e.g. '>100'), and store_failures to persist failing rows to a table. Community packages (dbt_utils, dbt_expectations) supply additional generic tests.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of dbt tests as a quality-control inspector standing at the end of your data pipeline with a checklist. Each check is phrased as 'show me the broken items': show me rows where the customer id is missing, show me duplicate order ids, show me statuses that are not one of the allowed words. The inspector runs each query - if it finds nothing broken, the check passes; if it pulls out even one bad row, the check fails and tells you how many. Generic checks are the standard reusable checklist items you attach to columns ('never empty', 'no duplicates'). Singular checks are custom one-off inspections you hand-write for a weird, specific rule. You tell the inspector how loud to be: 'stop the line' (error) or 'just note it' (warn).
coreConcept.historicalContext: dbt (data build tool) was created by Fishtown Analytics (now dbt Labs) beginning around 2016 to bring software-engineering practices - version control, modularity, and especially testing - to analytics SQL. From early on, dbt shipped four built-in schema tests (later called generic tests) - not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships - so analysts could assert data quality declaratively in YAML instead of writing bespoke checks. Over time the terminology settled: 'schema tests' became 'generic tests' and 'data tests' became 'singular tests' (with the dbt v1.8+ 'unit tests' added as a separate feature for testing model logic on mocked inputs). The community package dbt_utils added widely used tests like unique_combination_of_columns, expression_is_true, and accepted_range, while dbt_expectations (inspired by the Python Great Expectations library) brought a large catalog of statistical and distributional tests. Features like store_failures, the error_if/warn_if thresholds, and dbt build (which runs a model then immediately its tests) matured dbt into a data-quality gate that fits naturally into CI/CD.

whyItMatters.business: Tests protect the numbers executives and customers see. Catching a duplicated order or a null revenue field before it reaches a dashboard prevents wrong decisions and preserves trust in the data team - a single silently corrupted metric can erode confidence in every report.
whyItMatters.engineering: Tests turn tacit assumptions ('this key is unique', 'status is always one of these values') into executable, version-controlled assertions that fail loudly when violated, so regressions from upstream schema changes or bad loads are caught at build time instead of by a confused analyst weeks later.
whyItMatters.scalability: As a project grows to hundreds of models, generic tests declared in YAML give broad coverage cheaply, and packages add dozens more without custom code; store_failures and thresholds let large teams triage which failures actually block a release versus which are known, tolerable noise.
whyItMatters.cost: Failing fast in CI is far cheaper than debugging a wrong dashboard in production or re-running downstream pipelines on corrupted data; thresholds and warn severity avoid needlessly re-running expensive builds for trivial, expected imperfections.
whyItMatters.reliability: Tests are the reliability backbone of a dbt project: relationships tests guard referential integrity, unique/not_null guard primary keys, and singular tests encode business invariants, so the marts other systems depend on stay correct build after build.

coreComponents.name: Built-in generic tests (not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships)
coreComponents.definition: The four generic tests dbt ships out of the box, attached to a column or model in YAML: not_null asserts no NULLs, unique asserts no duplicate values, accepted_values asserts the column only contains a listed set of values, and relationships asserts every value exists in a referenced column of another model (referential integrity).
coreComponents.purpose: To assert the most common data-quality rules - primary key validity, allowed categories, and foreign-key integrity - declaratively without writing SQL.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Compile into failing-rows queries, validate keys and categories, enforce referential integrity across models, and run under dbt test / dbt build with configurable severity.
coreComponents.examples: columns: - name: order_id  tests: [unique, not_null]  |  - name: status  tests: - accepted_values: {values: ['placed','shipped','returned']}  |  - name: customer_id  tests: - relationships: {to: ref('stg_customers'), field: customer_id}

coreComponents.name: Custom generic tests
coreComponents.definition: User-defined generic tests written as macros (in a generic test block, typically under tests/generic/ or macros/) that take model and column_name arguments plus custom parameters and return a query selecting failing rows; they are then reusable across the project via YAML like any built-in test.
coreComponents.purpose: To make a project-specific rule reusable - write the failing-rows logic once and attach it to many columns/models by name.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Encapsulate a parameterized data-quality rule, accept arguments, return the failing-rows SELECT, and be invokable declaratively in YAML.
coreComponents.examples: {% test is_positive(model, column_name) %} select * from {{ model }} where {{ column_name }} <= 0 {% endtest %} then tests: [is_positive]

coreComponents.name: Singular tests (tests/ directory)
coreComponents.definition: One-off tests written as plain .sql files in the tests/ directory, each containing a SELECT that returns the rows considered failures; dbt runs the query as written, with no parameters or reuse.
coreComponents.purpose: To express complex or one-off business rules that do not generalize into a parameterized generic test.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Encode bespoke invariants (cross-model reconciliations, aggregate checks), return failing rows, and run alongside generic tests under dbt test / dbt build.
coreComponents.examples:
-- tests/assert_total_revenue_positive.sql
select order_date, sum(amount) as daily_total
from {{ ref('fct_orders') }}
group by 1
having sum(amount) < 0

coreComponents.name: Test configuration (severity, thresholds, store_failures)
coreComponents.definition: Per-test config controlling behavior: severity ('error' or 'warn'), error_if/warn_if numeric thresholds on the failing-row count (e.g. '>100'), store_failures to write failing rows to a table, and limit to cap rows returned.
coreComponents.purpose: To tune how failures affect the build and to make failures debuggable - deciding what blocks a release, what merely warns, and where failing rows are saved.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Set severity, apply count thresholds, persist failing rows for inspection, and control result limits per test or globally.
coreComponents.examples: tests: - unique: {config: {severity: warn}}  |  - not_null: {config: {severity: error, error_if: '>10', warn_if: '>0'}}  |  config: {store_failures: true}

coreComponents.name: Test packages (dbt_utils, dbt_expectations)
coreComponents.definition: Community macro packages installed via packages.yml and dbt deps that ship additional generic tests - dbt_utils adds tests like unique_combination_of_columns, expression_is_true, accepted_range, and not_null_proportion; dbt_expectations adds Great-Expectations-style tests such as expect_column_values_to_be_between and expect_column_values_to_match_regex.
coreComponents.purpose: To extend coverage with battle-tested, cross-database tests for multi-column keys, ranges, expressions, and statistical/distributional checks without writing them yourself.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Provide reusable generic tests for combinations, ranges, expressions, regex, and distributions, invoked in YAML with their namespace.

internalWorking: When you declare a generic test in YAML (e.g. tests: [not_null] on a column), dbt does not run your YAML directly - during parsing it looks up the corresponding test macro (test_not_null) and binds the model and column_name arguments (plus any extra params like values or to/field). It then compiles that macro into a concrete SQL query that selects the rows violating the assertion, and stores it as a node in the DAG that depends on the model being tested.

The compiled test query is structured to return failing rows. not_null compiles to roughly 'select * from model where column is null'; unique compiles to a group-by that returns values appearing more than once; accepted_values returns rows whose value is not in the allowed set; relationships returns child rows whose key has no match in the parent. dbt then wraps this in a counting query so it can report the number of failing rows.

At execution time (dbt test or dbt build), dbt runs each test query against the warehouse. It counts the returned rows: zero rows means PASS; one or more rows means FAIL (or WARN, depending on severity). The failing count is compared against error_if/warn_if thresholds if configured - so a test can be set to only fail when, say, more than 100 rows violate the rule, and merely warn when between 1 and 100 do.

Singular tests skip the macro layer: dbt reads the .sql file in tests/, compiles its Jinja (resolving ref/source), and runs the resulting SELECT as-is. Whatever rows the query returns are treated as failures. This is why a singular test's SQL must be written to return only the bad rows - a HAVING clause, a WHERE filter, or an anti-join that surfaces violations.

When store_failures is enabled, instead of only counting, dbt materializes the failing rows into a table (in a dedicated schema, typically <schema>_dbt_test__audit) so engineers can query exactly which records failed. During dbt build, a model's tests run immediately after the model is built, and if an error-severity test fails, dbt skips the model's downstream dependents - preventing bad data from propagating.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: YAML/SQL test definition -> parse phase (resolve generic test macro or read singular .sql, bind model/column args, add test node to DAG depending on model) -> compile phase (render failing-rows SQL to target/compiled/) -> execution (dbt test / dbt build runs each query) -> count failing rows -> compare to severity + error_if/warn_if thresholds -> PASS / WARN / FAIL result (optionally store_failures table) -> in dbt build, failing error-tests skip downstream models -> results surfaced in logs / CI
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. An analyst adds a schema.yml entry for fct_orders declaring order_id as unique and not_null, status with accepted_values, and customer_id with a relationships test to stg_customers, and writes a singular test file tests/assert_no_negative_revenue.sql.

2. dbt parses the project: it looks up test_unique, test_not_null, test_accepted_values, and test_relationships macros, binds their arguments (model=fct_orders, column_name=order_id, etc.), reads the singular test SQL, and adds each as a test node in the DAG depending on the relevant models.

3. dbt compiles each test into a failing-rows query written to target/compiled/ - for example the unique test becomes a group-by on order_id having count(*) > 1, and the relationships test becomes an anti-join finding customer_ids in fct_orders with no match in stg_customers.

4. On dbt build (or dbt test), dbt runs each query, counts returned rows, applies severity/thresholds, and reports PASS/WARN/FAIL; with store_failures on, failing rows land in an audit schema, and in dbt build an error-level failure on fct_orders skips models downstream of it so corrupted data does not propagate to marts consumed by dashboards.

keyTerminology.meaning: A parameterized, reusable test defined as a macro and applied declaratively in YAML under a model's or column's tests: key (built-in: not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships).
keyTerminology.importance: Generic tests give broad, cheap data-quality coverage across many columns and models with a single line of YAML each - the workhorse of dbt testing.

keyTerminology.meaning: A one-off test written as a .sql file in the tests/ directory whose SELECT returns the rows considered failures; run as-is with no parameters.
keyTerminology.importance: Singular tests handle complex, project-specific rules (cross-model reconciliations, aggregate invariants) that cannot be expressed as a reusable generic test.

keyTerminology.meaning: The core mechanic: every test compiles to a query that returns violating rows; zero rows returned = PASS, any rows = FAIL, and the failing count is reported.
keyTerminology.importance: Understanding that 'a test is a query for bad data' explains how to read results, write singular tests, and debug failures by inspecting the returned rows.

keyTerminology.meaning: severity decides whether a failing test errors (fails the build) or warns (reports but continues); error_if/warn_if set numeric conditions on the failing-row count (e.g. '>100') for finer control.
keyTerminology.importance: Thresholds and severity let teams distinguish build-blocking failures from tolerable noise, so CI fails only on issues that truly matter.

keyTerminology.meaning: A test config that writes the failing rows into a table (typically in a <schema>_dbt_test__audit schema) instead of only counting them.
keyTerminology.importance: It makes failures debuggable - you can query exactly which records violated the rule rather than only seeing a count.

importantConcepts.concept: A test is a query that returns failing rows
importantConcepts.explanation: The entire dbt testing model rests on one rule: every test - generic or singular - compiles into a SQL query, and dbt interprets the rows that query returns as violations. Zero rows means the assertion holds (PASS); any rows means it is broken (FAIL), and dbt reports the count. This is why writing a good singular test means writing SQL that surfaces only the bad rows - typically a WHERE filter for invalid values, a GROUP BY ... HAVING for duplicates or aggregate breaches, or an anti-join (LEFT JOIN ... WHERE parent.key IS NULL) for missing references. It also explains how built-ins work under the hood: unique is a group-by-having-count>1, relationships is an anti-join. Once you internalize 'a test returns the offenders', you can read any failure by inspecting those rows (especially with store_failures) and you can write custom logic confidently, because you always know what the query must produce.

importantConcepts.concept: Severity, thresholds, and where testing sits in the build
importantConcepts.explanation: Not every data imperfection should stop a release. dbt lets you set severity to 'error' (a failing test fails the build and, in dbt build, skips downstream models) or 'warn' (it reports but the build continues). For finer control, error_if and warn_if put conditions on the failing-row COUNT: for example error_if: '>100', warn_if: '>0' means the test warns on any failing rows but only errors when more than 100 fail. This is invaluable for known, tolerable noise (a handful of legacy bad records) versus a real regression (thousands suddenly failing). Because dbt build runs a model's tests immediately after building the model, error-level tests act as gates: they prevent corrupted data from flowing into dependent marts. In CI, this same mechanism turns tests into a merge gate - a pull request that introduces bad data or breaks an assumption fails the pipeline before it ever reaches production.

variationsAndTypes: **Built-in generic tests:** not_null (no NULLs), unique (no duplicates), accepted_values (value in an allowed set), relationships (referential integrity to another model's column).
**Custom generic tests:** user-written macros in a {% test %} block that take model/column_name plus params and return failing rows, reusable in YAML by name across the project.
**Singular tests:** bespoke .sql files in tests/ returning failing rows for a specific rule that does not generalize (cross-model reconciliation, aggregate invariants).
**Severity/threshold variants:** error vs warn severity, and error_if/warn_if conditions on the failing-row count for graduated responses.

**Package tests:** dbt_utils (unique_combination_of_columns, expression_is_true, accepted_range, not_null_proportion, etc.) and dbt_expectations (expect_column_values_to_be_between, _to_match_regex, _to_be_in_set, distributional checks).
**Related but distinct - unit tests:** dbt v1.8+ unit tests validate a model's SQL logic against mocked inputs/expected outputs, unlike data tests which validate the actual materialized data.
advantages: **Declarative coverage:** built-in generic tests give broad key/category/referential-integrity checks with a single line of YAML per column, so coverage scales cheaply.
**Version-controlled assertions:** tests encode assumptions in code that lives with the models, so intent is documented and regressions fail loudly at build time.
**Flexible severity:** error/warn plus error_if/warn_if thresholds let teams gate on real problems while tolerating known, minor noise.
**Debuggable failures:** store_failures persists the exact offending rows, and singular tests let you express any bespoke rule, so failures are inspectable and expressive.
**Extensible via packages:** dbt_utils and dbt_expectations add dozens of ready-made tests (ranges, regex, multi-column uniqueness, distributions) without custom code.
disadvantages: **Cost of running tests:** each test is a warehouse query; large tables with many tests add compute and runtime, so untuned testing can be expensive.
**False confidence:** tests only check what you assert - gaps in coverage (an untested column, a missing invariant) leave silent data-quality holes.
**Threshold tuning burden:** deciding error vs warn and setting error_if/warn_if requires judgment; poor tuning either blocks releases on noise or lets real issues warn silently.
**Point-in-time only:** data tests validate the data as materialized; they do not test model logic in isolation (that is what unit tests are for) and can miss logic bugs masked by current data.
**Maintenance:** relationships and accepted_values tests can become brittle as legitimate business changes (new statuses, expected orphans) require updating tests or they generate noise.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use generic tests liberally on primary keys (unique + not_null), on categorical columns (accepted_values), and on foreign keys (relationships); reach for package tests (dbt_utils, dbt_expectations) for multi-column keys, ranges, and distributions. Use singular tests for complex, one-off business invariants (cross-model reconciliations, aggregate sanity checks). Use warn severity and thresholds for known, tolerable imperfections, and store_failures whenever you need to debug which rows failed.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid over-testing giant tables with many redundant tests that inflate warehouse cost; avoid error severity on rules that are noisy or expected to occasionally break (use warn or thresholds instead); avoid singular tests when a generic or package test already expresses the rule; and do not rely on data tests to catch pure logic bugs that current data happens to mask - use unit tests for that.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: dbt tests are like quality control on a factory line. Generic tests are the standard, repeatable inspections stamped onto every product: 'no missing serial number' (not_null), 'no two products share a serial' (unique), 'color must be one of the approved swatches' (accepted_values), 'every part number matches the parts catalog' (relationships). Singular tests are the special inspections a supervisor hand-writes for a tricky rule specific to one product run. Each inspection is phrased as 'pull out the defective units' - if the bin of defects is empty, the batch passes; if anything lands in it, the batch fails and you can see exactly what was wrong (store_failures). Severity is the line policy: 'halt the line' (error) for serious defects versus 'log it and keep going' (warn) for cosmetic ones, and thresholds are the tolerance ('stop only if more than 100 defective').

commonMisconceptions.myth: A dbt test passes when its query returns rows, like a normal SELECT that 'found the data'.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It is the opposite. A test query is meant to return only the BAD rows; zero rows means PASS, and any returned rows mean FAIL. You write test SQL to surface violations, not to confirm data exists.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The four built-in tests are enough for real data quality.
commonMisconceptions.reality: not_null, unique, accepted_values, and relationships cover key/category/referential rules, but real projects need ranges, multi-column uniqueness, regex, freshness, and business invariants - hence custom generic tests, singular tests, and packages like dbt_utils and dbt_expectations.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Attach generic tests broadly but be deliberate on very large tables - each test is a full query; prefer package tests over hand-rolled SQL for consistency, and consider testing incrementally or on samples in dev while running full tests in CI/prod.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Gate marts with error-severity tests on primary keys and referential integrity so bad data fails the build; use dbt build so a failing test skips downstream models and prevents corrupted data from propagating to consumers.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Use warn severity and error_if/warn_if thresholds for known, tolerable imperfections so transient or legacy noise does not block every release; enable store_failures on critical tests so failures can be triaged from persisted rows rather than re-running.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Surface test results in CI and in run artifacts (run_results.json); alert on error-level failures, and track warn-level counts over time to spot degrading data quality before it crosses a threshold.
productionConsiderations.security: Restrict access to the dbt_test__audit (store_failures) schema since it can contain raw failing records including sensitive values; avoid storing failures of PII-heavy tables, or mask them.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Consolidate overlapping tests, avoid redundant not_null on already-unique keys where appropriate, use thresholds instead of re-running, and run the heaviest tests in CI on changed models (state:modified) rather than the whole project every time.
productionConsiderations.performance: Prefer set-based test SQL (group-by/anti-join) that the warehouse optimizes well; use limit on store_failures to cap audit-table size, and select only relevant tests (dbt test --select) during iterative development instead of the full suite.

codeExamples.title: Applying the four built-in generic tests in schema.yml
codeExamples.overview: A models/marts/schema.yml declaring not_null and unique on a primary key, accepted_values on a categorical column, and relationships for referential integrity - with a warn severity and a threshold example.
codeExamples.code:
version: 2

models:
  - name: fct_orders
    description: "One row per order with revenue in dollars."
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        description: "Primary key."
        tests:
          - unique
          - not_null

      - name: status
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['placed', 'shipped', 'returned', 'cancelled']

      - name: customer_id
        tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              to: ref('stg_customers')
              field: customer_id

      - name: amount_usd
        tests:
          - not_null:
              config:
                severity: warn
                warn_if: ">0"
                error_if: ">100"
codeExamples.breakdown: Under models: each model lists columns: and their tests:. order_id gets unique + not_null (a primary-key check). status uses accepted_values with an explicit values list. customer_id uses relationships with to: (the parent model via ref) and field: (the parent column) to enforce foreign-key integrity. amount_usd shows per-test config: severity warn plus thresholds - warn_if '>0' reports any nulls but error_if '>100' only fails the build when more than 100 rows are null.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: dbt test runs one query per test. Passing tests log e.g. 'PASS unique_fct_orders_order_id'. A failure logs 'FAIL 3 unique_fct_orders_order_id' meaning 3 duplicate order_ids were found. The relationships test fails with the count of customer_ids in fct_orders that have no match in stg_customers.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting ref() in relationships (using a bare table name) breaks resolution. Listing accepted_values that omit a legitimate new status causes spurious failures. Putting config keys at the wrong indentation level (config: must nest under the test) is a common YAML error.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use warn + thresholds for columns with known, tolerable nulls; reserve error severity for true primary keys and referential integrity. Group all tests for a model in one schema.yml near the model file for discoverability.

codeExamples.title: A custom generic test and a singular test
codeExamples.overview: A reusable custom generic test (is_positive) written as a macro, applied in YAML, plus a singular test file that reconciles a business invariant across a model.
codeExamples.code:
-- tests/generic/test_is_positive.sql
{% test is_positive(model, column_name) %}
select *
from {{ model }}
where {{ column_name }} <= 0
  and {{ column_name }} is not null
{% endtest %}


-- Applied in schema.yml:
-- columns:
--   - name: amount_usd
--     tests:
--       - is_positive


-- tests/assert_daily_revenue_non_negative.sql  (singular test)
select
    order_date,
    sum(amount_usd) as daily_total
from {{ ref('fct_orders') }}
group by order_date
having sum(amount_usd) < 0
codeExamples.breakdown: The {% test name(model, column_name) %}...{% endtest %} block defines a generic test; model and column_name are auto-supplied by dbt from where you apply it, and the body returns rows where the value is <= 0 (the failing rows). Once defined, it is reusable in YAML as just 'is_positive'. The singular test is a plain .sql file in tests/: it groups fct_orders by day and uses HAVING to return only days whose total revenue is negative - any returned row is a failure. Both rely on the 'return the bad rows' contract.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: is_positive passes when no non-null amount_usd is <= 0; otherwise it fails with the count of offending rows. The singular test passes when every day's revenue is non-negative and fails listing the specific order_dates with negative totals.
codeExamples.commonIssues: In the generic test, forgetting to exclude NULLs (which are neither > 0 nor <= 0) can produce surprising results - decide explicitly how NULLs should behave. In singular tests, accidentally returning ALL rows (no HAVING/WHERE filter) makes the test always fail. Placing a generic test file outside tests/generic or macros/ means dbt will not discover it.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Parameterize custom generic tests (add optional min_value arguments) to maximize reuse. Keep singular tests focused on one invariant each so a failure points clearly at the broken rule.

codeExamples.title: Running tests and storing failures from the CLI
codeExamples.overview: Day-to-day commands to run tests, run them interleaved with builds, target specific tests, install test packages, and persist failing rows for debugging.
codeExamples.code:
# Run every test in the project
dbt test

# Run only tests on one model (and its columns)
dbt test --select fct_orders

# Build models AND run their tests interleaved (tests gate downstream models)
dbt build

# Store failing rows to an audit table for debugging
dbt test --select fct_orders --store-failures

# In CI: run only tests on models changed in this PR
dbt build --select state:modified+ --state ./prod-artifacts

# Install dbt_utils / dbt_expectations declared in packages.yml
dbt deps
codeExamples.breakdown: dbt test executes all test queries and reports PASS/WARN/FAIL with counts. --select scopes to one model's tests. dbt build runs each model then its tests in DAG order, so an error-severity test failure skips downstream models. --store-failures writes failing rows to the <schema>_dbt_test__audit schema so you can query them. state:modified+ with --state points at prior artifacts so CI only tests changed models and their children. dbt deps installs packages listed in packages.yml so their generic tests become available.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: dbt test prints a summary like 'Done. PASS=42 WARN=1 ERROR=2 SKIP=0 TOTAL=45' and per-test lines. With --store-failures, failing rows appear in a table like analytics_dbt_test__audit.unique_fct_orders_order_id you can SELECT to inspect.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Running dbt test before dbt run on a fresh warehouse fails because the models do not exist yet - use dbt build or run models first. Forgetting dbt deps means package tests (dbt_utils.*, dbt_expectations.*) are undefined and parsing fails. Not passing --state in CI causes state:modified to select everything.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use dbt build in CI so tests gate the build; scope with --select / state:modified+ to test only what changed; enable --store-failures selectively on tests you actively debug rather than globally to control audit-schema growth.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A retail analytics team keeps shipping dashboards that occasionally show duplicated orders, revenue totals that go negative after a bad load, and orders pointing at deleted customers. They need automated data-quality gates so these defects fail a pull request in CI before they ever reach production marts.
endToEndExample.inputData: Staging models stg_orders (order_id, customer_id, status, amount_usd, order_date) and stg_customers (customer_id, ...), built from raw source tables loaded by an EL tool; a marts model fct_orders built on top of stg_orders.
endToEndExample.architecture: Generic tests in schema.yml enforce a unique+not_null primary key on order_id, accepted_values on status, and a relationships test from fct_orders.customer_id to stg_customers.customer_id; a custom generic test is_positive guards amount_usd; a singular test reconciles daily revenue to be non-negative; dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns guards a composite key on the line-item model. dbt build runs models then tests, and CI runs it on every PR.
processingSteps: 1. Declare dbt_utils and dbt_expectations in packages.yml and run dbt deps so their generic tests are available.
2. Add schema.yml tests: unique + not_null on order_id, accepted_values on status, relationships on customer_id, and not_null with warn+threshold on amount_usd for known legacy nulls.

3. Write a custom generic test is_positive (macro returning rows where amount_usd <= 0) and apply it to amount_usd; write a singular test tests/assert_daily_revenue_non_negative.sql returning days with negative totals.

4. Set severity: error on the primary-key and relationships tests (build-blocking) and warn (with error_if thresholds) on softer rules; enable store_failures on the relationships test to debug orphaned orders.
5. Configure CI to run dbt build --select state:modified+ on each pull request so only changed models and their children are built and tested, failing the PR if any error-severity test fails.
endToEndExample.output: A CI pipeline where every pull request builds the affected models and runs their tests; PASS results allow the merge, while a duplicated order_id, an orphaned customer_id, or negative daily revenue produces a FAIL that blocks the merge and points (via store_failures) at the exact offending rows.
endToEndExample.monitoring: run_results.json from each dbt build is parsed in CI to report pass/warn/fail counts; error-level failures block the merge and notify the team, and warn-level counts are tracked over time to catch slowly degrading quality before it crosses an error threshold.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: warn severity plus error_if/warn_if thresholds absorb known, tolerable noise without blocking every release; store_failures persists offending rows into an audit schema so engineers triage from data rather than re-running; because dbt build interleaves tests, an error on fct_orders skips its downstream models so bad data never reaches dependent marts.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Data-quality defects are caught at the pull-request stage instead of in production dashboards: primary keys stay unique, statuses stay valid, orders always reference real customers, and revenue never silently goes negative - all enforced automatically, with failing rows readily inspectable when something does break.

industryUseCases.problem: Order and customer marts intermittently contain duplicate order ids and orphaned foreign keys after messy upstream loads, corrupting revenue dashboards.
industryUseCases.solution: Apply unique + not_null on primary keys and relationships tests on foreign keys with error severity, run via dbt build in CI so failures block merges.
industryUseCases.benefits: Duplicates and orphaned references are caught before production, revenue figures stay trustworthy, and the offending rows are inspectable via store_failures.

industryUseCases.problem: Monetary and status fields must obey strict invariants (amounts non-negative, statuses within an allowed lifecycle, balances reconciling) or downstream ledgers break.
industryUseCases.solution: Use accepted_values for status lifecycles, custom generic tests and dbt_expectations range tests for amounts, and singular tests for cross-table balance reconciliation, all at error severity.
industryUseCases.benefits: Financial invariants are enforced automatically, regulatory-grade correctness is documented as code, and reconciliation breaks fail the build rather than the auditor.

industryUseCases.company: SaaS data platforms with large, evolving schemas
industryUseCases.problem: Hundreds of models with composite keys and range-bounded metrics are impossible to hand-check, and new columns/statuses constantly appear.
industryUseCases.solution: Lean on dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns, accepted_range, and dbt_expectations distributional tests declared broadly in YAML, tuned with warn/thresholds for expected variability.
industryUseCases.benefits: Broad, low-effort coverage across many models, graceful handling of evolving data via thresholds, and consistent cross-database test behavior from packages.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Generic tests scale coverage cheaply via one YAML line each, but every test is a warehouse query - on very large tables, scope tests with --select/state:modified+ in CI, prefer package tests over redundant hand-written SQL, and consider sampling in dev while running the full suite in CI/prod.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Use warn severity and error_if/warn_if thresholds so known, tolerable imperfections do not block every build; enable store_failures on critical tests so a failure can be triaged from persisted rows without re-running; run tests via dbt build so a failing error-test skips downstream models rather than corrupting them.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Because tests are compiled SQL nodes in the DAG, they run deterministically alongside models and can be re-issued from artifacts; gating marts with error-severity primary-key and referential tests keeps dependent systems consuming only validated data.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Version-control all tests (schema.yml, tests/, custom generic macros) and pin dbt_utils/dbt_expectations versions in packages.yml so the exact test behavior is reproducible; store_failures audit tables provide a forensic record of what failed and when.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Favor set-based test SQL (group-by/anti-join) the warehouse optimizes well; cap store_failures with a limit; avoid redundant tests (e.g. not_null on a column already covered by a stricter test); and run only changed-model tests during iterative development.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Run heavy tests in CI on state:modified+ rather than the whole project each time; use thresholds instead of re-running to tolerate noise; consolidate overlapping tests; and reserve expensive package tests (distributions, regex over huge tables) for where they add real value.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: The store_failures audit schema can contain raw failing records including PII - restrict access, avoid storing failures on sensitive tables or mask them, and treat the dbt_test__audit schema with the same governance as production data.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Parse run_results.json in CI for pass/warn/fail counts, alert on any error-severity failure, and trend warn-level failing counts over time to detect data quality degrading before it crosses an error threshold.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Combine built-in generic tests (keys, categories, referential integrity), custom generic tests (project rules), singular tests (business invariants), and package tests (ranges, multi-column keys, distributions) to cover the full spectrum of assertions on materialized data.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Emit test results to CI logs and dashboards; block merges on error-level failures with clear messages pointing at the failing test and (via store_failures) the offending rows, and route warn-level trends to a data-quality channel for proactive attention.

recommendedPractices: **Always test primary and foreign keys:** put unique + not_null on every model's primary key and a relationships test on every foreign key at error severity.
**Write test SQL to return only bad rows:** for singular and custom generic tests, use WHERE/HAVING/anti-joins so a failure means the query surfaced violations.
**Use dbt build, not just dbt run + dbt test:** so tests gate downstream models and bad data is not propagated.
**Tune severity and thresholds deliberately:** error for build-blocking invariants, warn + error_if/warn_if for known, tolerable noise.
engineeringStandards: Keep each model's tests in a schema.yml next to the model file for discoverability, and store singular tests in tests/ and custom generic tests in tests/generic/ or macros/.
Always use ref()/source() inside singular and generic test SQL so dependencies and environment resolution stay correct.
Pin dbt_utils and dbt_expectations versions in packages.yml and run dbt deps so package test behavior is reproducible.
designRecommendations: Prefer built-in and package generic tests before writing custom SQL; reach for singular tests only for genuinely bespoke, non-generalizable invariants.
Parameterize custom generic tests (optional arguments) so a single test covers many columns and models.
Reserve error severity for correctness-critical rules and use warn/thresholds elsewhere to keep CI signal-to-noise high.
namingConventions: Let dbt's auto-generated test names stand (e.g. unique_fct_orders_order_id) unless you need a custom name via the name: config for clarity.
Name singular test files after the invariant they check (assert_daily_revenue_non_negative.sql) so failures are self-describing.
Name custom generic tests as clear predicates (is_positive, is_valid_email) that read naturally in YAML.
documentationStandards: Document in the column/model description why each non-obvious test exists (especially accepted_values lists and thresholds) so future maintainers understand intent.
Note in package/config comments why a test warns rather than errors, or why a threshold was chosen.
Record custom generic test arguments and NULL-handling behavior so reuse is unambiguous.
testingStrategies: Cover keys (unique/not_null), categories (accepted_values), and references (relationships) as a baseline on every mart.
Add package tests for ranges, multi-column uniqueness, and distributions, and singular tests for cross-model reconciliations.
Run the full suite in CI via dbt build on state:modified+ so every PR is gated on the tests relevant to its changes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing singular/custom test SQL that returns rows on success instead of returning only the failing rows.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers think of a test as 'select the data I expect', forgetting that dbt treats any returned row as a failure.
commonMistakes.impact: The test either always fails (returns all rows) or always passes (never returns the offenders), giving false results and eroding trust in the suite.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Write the query to return ONLY violations - use WHERE for invalid values, GROUP BY ... HAVING for duplicates/aggregate breaches, and anti-joins for missing references - so zero rows means pass.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting every test to error severity, including noisy or expected-imperfect rules.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Error is the default and feels safest, so teams never revisit severity as the project and data mature.
commonMistakes.impact: CI fails constantly on known, tolerable noise, engineers start ignoring or disabling tests, and real failures get lost in the alarm fatigue.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Reserve error for correctness-critical invariants (keys, referential integrity); use warn plus error_if/warn_if thresholds for rules with known, acceptable imperfections.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running dbt run and dbt test as separate steps instead of dbt build.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Older tutorials teach run-then-test, and teams keep the two-step habit.
commonMistakes.impact: Downstream models get built on top of a model whose tests fail, so corrupted data propagates before the test step even runs.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use dbt build, which runs each model then immediately its tests in DAG order, so an error-severity failure skips the model's dependents and stops bad data from spreading.

comparisonSection.optionA: Generic test (parameterized macro, applied in YAML)
comparisonSection.optionB: Singular test (one-off SQL file in tests/)
comparisonSection.explanation: A generic test is reusable and declarative - defined once (built-in or as a macro) and attached to many columns/models with a line of YAML, ideal for common rules like keys, categories, and references. A singular test is a single bespoke SQL query for a rule that does not generalize, such as a cross-model reconciliation or an aggregate invariant. Use generic tests for the repeatable majority of checks; use singular tests only for the specific, complex logic that cannot be parameterized into a generic test.

comparisonSection.feature: Handling a test that finds some failing rows
comparisonSection.optionA: severity: error (fails the build, skips downstream in dbt build)
comparisonSection.optionB: severity: warn (reports but continues) + error_if/warn_if thresholds
comparisonSection.explanation: error treats any failing row as a build-blocking failure, right for correctness-critical invariants like primary keys and referential integrity where even one bad row is unacceptable. warn reports the failure without failing the build, and error_if/warn_if add graduated conditions on the failing-row count (e.g. warn on any, error only above 100) for rules with known, tolerable noise. Choose error to gate releases on true invariants and warn+thresholds to tolerate expected imperfections without alarm fatigue.

beginnerQuestions.question: What are the four built-in generic tests in dbt and what does each assert?
beginnerQuestions.answer: not_null asserts a column has no NULL values; unique asserts a column has no duplicate values; accepted_values asserts a column only contains values from a specified allowed list; and relationships asserts that every value in a column exists in a referenced column of another model, enforcing referential (foreign-key) integrity.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: These cover the most common rules: not_null + unique validate primary keys, accepted_values validates categorical columns, and relationships validates foreign keys. Mention they are declared in YAML under a column's tests: key.

beginnerQuestions.question: How does dbt decide whether a test passes or fails?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Every test compiles into a SQL query that selects the rows violating the assertion. dbt runs the query and counts the returned rows: zero rows means PASS, and one or more rows means FAIL (dbt reports the failing count). So a test is essentially a query for bad data.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The key insight is the 'zero-rows-pass' model - the query returns offenders, not confirmations. This is why singular tests must be written to return only the bad rows.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between a generic test and a singular test?
intermediateQuestions.answer: A generic test is a parameterized, reusable test defined as a macro (built-in or custom) and applied declaratively in YAML to many columns/models - e.g. unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships. A singular test is a one-off .sql file in the tests/ directory containing a specific SELECT that returns failing rows, run as-is with no parameters or reuse. Generic tests cover repeatable rules; singular tests express bespoke, non-generalizable invariants.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Emphasize reusability vs specificity, and that a custom generic test is written as a {% test %} macro taking model and column_name, whereas a singular test is plain SQL.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do severity and the error_if/warn_if thresholds work?
intermediateQuestions.answer: severity is 'error' (a failing test fails the build) or 'warn' (it reports but the build continues). error_if and warn_if place numeric conditions on the failing-row count - for example warn_if: '>0', error_if: '>100' means the test warns on any failing rows but only errors when more than 100 fail. This lets teams distinguish build-blocking issues from known, tolerable noise.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Connect to CI: error-severity tests gate merges, while warn+thresholds tolerate expected imperfections without alarm fatigue. In dbt build, an error failure also skips downstream models.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you write a custom generic test, and how does dbt know which model and column to test?
advancedQuestions.answer: Define it as a macro in a {% test name(model, column_name) %}...{% endtest %} block (in tests/generic/ or macros/) whose body returns the failing rows, e.g. select * from {{ model }} where {{ column_name }} <= 0. dbt automatically supplies the model relation and column_name based on where you apply the test in YAML (which model, which column). You can add extra parameters (e.g. min_value) that callers pass in YAML. Once defined, it is reusable by name across the project.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Show that model and column_name are special auto-bound arguments and that the macro must return only violating rows to honor the zero-rows-pass contract.

advancedQuestions.question: What does store_failures do, and when would you use it? How do packages like dbt_expectations extend testing?
advancedQuestions.answer: store_failures makes dbt materialize the failing rows into a table (in a <schema>_dbt_test__audit schema) instead of only counting them, so you can query exactly which records failed - invaluable for debugging referential or complex failures. dbt_utils and dbt_expectations are macro packages adding many generic tests: dbt_utils gives unique_combination_of_columns, expression_is_true, accepted_range; dbt_expectations gives Great-Expectations-style tests like expect_column_values_to_be_between, _to_match_regex, and distributional checks - installed via packages.yml + dbt deps and used in YAML with their namespace.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrates depth: you know how to debug failures (store_failures, limit) and how to extend coverage beyond the four built-ins for ranges, multi-column keys, regex, and distributions.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A teammate wrote a singular test tests/check_orders.sql as 'select * from {{ ref("fct_orders") }} where status = "shipped"', and now the test fails on every run even though shipped orders are perfectly valid. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: dbt treats any rows a test query returns as failures. This query returns all shipped orders - which are valid - so dbt sees thousands of 'failing' rows and reports FAIL. The author confused 'select the data I want' with 'select the bad rows'. A test must return ONLY violations.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Rewrite the query to return only invalid rows. If the intent was 'status must be one of an allowed set', replace it with an accepted_values generic test in YAML, or a singular test like 'select * from {{ ref('fct_orders') }} where status not in (\'placed\',\'shipped\',\'returned\',\'cancelled\')'. Verify it returns zero rows when data is clean. The principle: zero rows returned = PASS, so the query must surface only offenders.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a data-quality gate for a dbt project of ~200 models feeding executive dashboards, so that bad data (duplicate keys, orphaned references, out-of-range or invalid values) fails a pull request in CI before reaching production, while tolerating a small amount of known, legacy imperfection.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Baseline every mart with unique+not_null on primary keys, relationships on foreign keys, and accepted_values on categoricals at error severity. Add package tests (dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns, accepted_range; dbt_expectations range/regex/distribution tests) for composite keys and numeric bounds, and singular tests for cross-model reconciliations. Use warn + error_if/warn_if thresholds for columns with known, tolerable noise. Run dbt build so tests gate downstream models, and enable store_failures on critical tests for debugging.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: More tests mean broader coverage but more warehouse cost and runtime; error severity everywhere maximizes safety but risks alarm fatigue and blocked releases on noise. Balance by reserving error for true invariants, using warn/thresholds for the rest, and scoping CI to changed models to control cost.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Run CI on dbt build --select state:modified+ with --state pointing at prod artifacts so only changed models and their children are tested; prefer package tests over redundant hand-written SQL; cap store_failures with limits; and trend warn-level counts over time to catch degradation before it crosses an error threshold.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: dbt tests are data-quality assertions compiled into SQL queries that return failing rows (zero rows = PASS); generic tests (not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships, custom, and package tests) are reusable YAML-applied macros, while singular tests are one-off SQL files, all run via dbt test / dbt build with configurable severity and thresholds.
keyConcepts: A test is a query for bad rows: zero rows returned = PASS, any rows = FAIL (count reported).
Four built-in generic tests: not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships.
Custom generic tests are {% test(model, column_name) %} macros; singular tests are .sql files in tests/.
severity: error (fails/blocks) vs warn (reports); error_if/warn_if set count thresholds like '>100'.
store_failures persists offending rows to a <schema>_dbt_test__audit table for debugging.
interviewPoints: Zero-rows-pass: a test query returns only the violating rows.
Built-ins: not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships (referential integrity).
Generic (reusable, YAML) vs singular (one-off SQL in tests/).
severity error/warn + error_if/warn_if thresholds gate CI on real issues only.
dbt_utils and dbt_expectations add range, multi-column, regex, and distribution tests.
quickNotes: Use dbt build so tests gate downstream models; an error test skips dependents.
relationships needs to: ref('parent') and field: parent_column.
Write singular test SQL with WHERE/HAVING/anti-join to return only offenders.
Pin package versions in packages.yml and run dbt deps for reproducible tests.
store_failures schema can contain PII - restrict access and govern it.

keyTakeaways: Every dbt test compiles into a SQL query that returns the failing rows: zero rows means PASS, any rows means FAIL - internalizing this 'query for bad data' model is the key to reading results and writing tests correctly.

Generic tests are reusable, YAML-applied macros (built-in not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships, plus custom ones you write as {% test %} macros), while singular tests are one-off SQL files in tests/ for bespoke, non-generalizable invariants.

Control how failures behave with severity (error fails and, in dbt build, skips downstream; warn reports) and error_if/warn_if thresholds on the failing-row count, so CI gates on real problems and tolerates known noise.

Run tests with dbt test or, better, dbt build (which interleaves tests to gate downstream models), scope CI to changed models with state:modified+, and use store_failures to persist offending rows for debugging.

Extend coverage beyond the four built-ins with dbt_utils (unique_combination_of_columns, expression_is_true, accepted_range) and dbt_expectations (ranges, regex, distributions), installed via packages.yml and dbt deps.
